docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Generated by Nikhil Kumar Rajput

A survey of the silicon, firmware and appliances that secure a data centre, from the campus fence to the transistor: roots of trust, TPMs, HSMs, TEEs, encrypted links, post-quantum migration and who supplies them.

docs.title: Chapter 5: A Taxonomy of Data-Centre Security IP
docs.text: With the facility and the threats in view, we can now name the building blocks. Most of them are delivered as licensable silicon IP integrated into SoCs, as discrete chips on the board, or as firmware running on either, and the same function, for example a root of trust, can appear in all three forms in one server. This chapter defines each class of security IP, then explains the roles into which standards divide the root of trust and why a server contains more than one.

docs.title: 5.2 Roles of the root of trust
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-193 and the TCG split "the root of trust" into roles, and one chip may implement several of them. Distinguishing the roles explains why a server contains more than one RoT.

Role Responsibility Typical home RTM: Root of Trust for Measurement Takes the first measurement of mutable code CPU boot ROM and microcode, Caliptra core, DICE engine RTS: Root of Trust for Storage Shielded storage of keys and measurements TPM, Caliptra key and PCR vaults, OpenTitan OTP and flash RTR: Root of Trust for Reporting Signs measurement reports (quotes, SPDM measurements) TPM, Caliptra runtime, GPU and NIC firmware RTU: Root of Trust for Update Authenticates firmware updates and prevents rollback PRoT, BMC, Caliptra MCU, device ROM RTRec: Root of Trust for Recovery Restores known-good firmware after corruption PRoT with golden image, OCP Recovery and streaming boot RTD: Root of Trust for Detection Detects corruption at boot and at run time PRoT SPI and SMBus monitors, BMC, fleet attestation

docs.title: 5.3 Discrete versus integrated
docs.text: A discrete platform RoT is a separate chip that can hold other chips in reset and physically interpose on their flash. It protects devices that lack their own RoT and it survives a compromised host. An integrated RoT sits inside the SoC boundary, so it can measure the SoC's own firmware and protect keys from board-level probing. The industry direction, championed by OCP and Caliptra, is an integrated RoT in every major chip, plus a platform RoT that aggregates and attests them.

docs.title: 5.4 Summary
docs.text:
• Security IP comes as licensable silicon IP, discrete chips or firmware, and one function (such as a root of trust) can appear in all three forms in one server.
  • The classes include RoTs, boot ROMs, DICE, TPMs, HSMs, key stores, crypto and PQC accelerators, memory and link encryption, TEEs, attestation responders, lifecycle control, anti-tamper and secure management controllers.
  • NIST SP 800-193 and TCG split the RoT into roles: measurement, storage, reporting, update, recovery and detection.
  • A discrete RoT holds other chips in reset and survives a compromised host; an integrated RoT measures its own SoC. The direction is both: an integrated RoT in every chip plus a platform RoT that aggregates them.

docs.title: 5.5 Exercises
docs.text:
1. What does the RTM role do, and where does it typically live?

    Answer

    The Root of Trust for Measurement takes the first measurement of mutable code. It lives in the CPU boot ROM and microcode, the Caliptra core or a DICE engine.

  2. Why does a server contain more than one root of trust?

    Answer

    Different roles and different chips need different anchors: a discrete platform RoT protects the flash of devices that lack their own, integrated RoTs measure each SoC, and a TPM or HSM holds sealed keys. One chip may implement several roles, but no single one covers all of them.

  3. State one advantage of a discrete PRoT and one of an integrated RoT.

    Answer

    Discrete: it can hold other chips in reset and interpose on their flash, protecting devices without their own RoT and surviving a compromised host. Integrated: it can measure the SoC's own firmware and protect keys from board-level probing.

  4. Which class of security IP converts a device secret and code measurements into a per-boot identity?

    Answer

    The DICE engine, which derives compound device identifiers (CDIs) from the unique device secret and measurements of the code.

docs.title: Chapter 3: AI Data Centres: The AI Factory
docs.text: An AI data centre is built around accelerator clusters whose performance depends on moving enormous volumes of data between GPUs with microsecond latency. This changes almost every layer of the stack in Chapter 1: rack density rises by 10 to 50 times, liquid cooling becomes mandatory, three or four separate networks appear, and the most valuable asset becomes the model weights, the distilled result of hundreds of millions of dollars of compute. This chapter describes the AI factory, its topology and the anatomy of an NVL72-class rack, and lists the security features built into each accelerator platform.

docs.title: 3.1 How AI changes the facility
docs.text: Dimension Conventional cloud or enterprise AI training or inference data centre Rack density 5 to 20 kW, air-cooled 40 to 140 kW (GB200 and GB300 NVL72 about 120 to 140 kW); roadmap about 600 kW with direct liquid cooling Unit of compute Server or VM Rack-scale scale-up domain (72 GPUs on NVLink, 72 MI455X in AMD Helios, TPU pods, Trainium UltraServers) Networks Front-end and out-of-band Front-end, back-end scale-out (InfiniBand or Ethernet RDMA), scale-up (NVLink or UALink), storage, out-of-band, plus facility OT Traffic North-south dominated East-west dominated: all-reduce collectives, checkpoint bursts of many TB Power 10 to 100 MW 100 MW to multi-GW campuses; on-site generation, battery storage; 800 VDC distribution emerging Crown jewels Customer data, credentials Model weights, training data and recipes, checkpoints, RLHF data, prompts and outputs, tenant keys Tenancy Many tenants per server Often one lab per cluster (training) or many tenants per GPU (inference, MIG) Key security IP CPU RoT, TPM, CPU TEEs Plus GPU RoT and TEE, NVLink and IDE link encryption, DPU RoT, attested inference, HSM-gated weight keys

docs.title: 3.2 The logical topology of an AI factory
docs.text:
Figure 3.1 shows the logical topology. Several scale-up domains (each a set of GPUs joined by NVLink, UALink or Infinity Fabric switch trays, with a CPU, a BMC with platform RoT, and a DPU or SuperNIC) are joined by a back-end scale-out fabric (InfiniBand XDR, Spectrum-X or Ultra Ethernet, rail-optimised, RDMA). Around them sit a front-end Ethernet fabric for tenant networks, storage access and control traffic; a storage tier (parallel file system, NVMe-oF, object store, self-encrypting drives); control and trust services (scheduler, KMS and HSM for key custody, attestation verifier, SIEM and firmware inventory); an isolated out-of-band management network (BMCs, rack managers, PDUs, CDUs, switch management ports, jump hosts); and facility OT segmented per IEC 62443 zones and conduits. At the edge are DDoS scrubbing, WAF, firewalls and API gateways.

Figure 3.1. Logical topology of an AI factory: scale-up domains joined by a back-end fabric, front-end and storage networks, an isolated out-of-band management network and facility OT, with security-IP badges.

docs.title: 3.3 Anatomy of an NVL72-class rack
docs.text:
Figure 3.2 opens up one rack. Power shelves and battery backup hold PSU microcontrollers on PMBus, with signed firmware and PRoT-supervised updates; a compromised power shelf is a denial-of-service and fire-safety risk. Each of the 18 compute trays carries two Grace or Vera CPUs and four Blackwell or Rubin GPUs (or EPYC and MI4xx in AMD Helios); each GPU has an on-die root of trust, secure and measured boot, a fused device identity and a confidential-computing mode, and each CPU has an integrated security processor, a TEE and memory encryption. The tray's BMC and platform RoT sit on a DC-SCM, with a TPM, SuperNICs and a BlueField DPU. Nine NVLink switch trays hold switch ASICs that run no tenant code, with secure boot, signed firmware and SPDM attestation; NVLink traffic is encrypted end to end on Rubin-generation systems, and UALink 1.0 defines UALinkSec as the open alternative. The liquid manifold and CDU controllers are networked OT needing signed firmware, IEC 62443-4-2 and segmentation. The 48 to 54 V or 800 V DC busbar carries its own controllers for electrical safety and power capping. A rack manager and management switch aggregate tray BMCs, leak sensors and CDU telemetry using mutual-TLS Redfish, MACsec on management links and role-based access control, on an isolated out-of-band network.

Figure 3.2. Anatomy of an NVL72-class AI rack with the security functions of each element.

docs.title: 3.5 Summary
docs.text:
• AI factories raise rack density 10 to 50 times, make liquid cooling mandatory and add scale-up, scale-out, storage and out-of-band networks.
  • The crown jewels become model weights, training data, checkpoints, prompts and outputs, and tenant keys.
  • In an NVL72-class rack, every element, even a power shelf or a coolant distribution unit, has its own controller and a security function.
  • Each accelerator family brings its own RoT, boot security and confidential-computing support, with NVIDIA, AMD and the hyperscaler designs at different stages of rack-scale protection.

docs.title: 3.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. List the networks of an AI factory and say which is dominated by east-west traffic.

    Answer

    Front-end (north-south), back-end scale-out (InfiniBand or Ethernet RDMA), scale-up (NVLink or UALink), storage, out-of-band management, plus facility OT. The back-end and scale-up fabrics are east-west dominated: all-reduce collectives and checkpoint bursts of many terabytes.

  2. Why are NVLink switch trays described as running "no tenant code", and which security features do they still need?

    Answer

    Their ASICs only switch traffic; tenants do not run software on them. They still need secure boot, signed firmware and SPDM attestation, and NVLink traffic is encrypted end to end on Rubin-generation systems.

  3. Which GPU generation first introduced a GPU TEE, and how did it protect the CPU-GPU channel?

    Answer

    NVIDIA Hopper (H100). It used a CC mode with AES-GCM encrypted PCIe bounce buffers, whose keys are negotiated via SPDM.

  4. Why is a power shelf with a compromised PSU microcontroller a security risk, not just a reliability one?

    Answer

    The PSU microcontrollers run firmware on PMBus; a compromise can cause denial of service and is a fire-safety risk. That is why they need signed firmware, OCP recovery and PRoT-supervised updates.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Confidential Computing for AI
docs.text: Confidential computing protects data in use by running workloads in hardware-isolated trusted execution environments whose memory is encrypted and whose configuration can be remotely attested before any secret is released. For AI this means that model weights and prompts can be processed on infrastructure the owner does not control, which matters for cloud-hosted frontier models, multi-party training and regulated inference. This chapter covers CPU TEEs, accelerator TEEs and trusted I/O, the attestation flow of confidential inference, the services and software that support it, and its limits.

docs.text: Technology Vendor Isolation unit Memory protection Attestation root Trusted I/O SGX Intel Process enclave MEE or TME-MK; integrity on early parts Intel-provisioned keys, DCAP n/a TDX 1.x and 2.x Intel (4th-generation Xeon onwards; GA on 5th generation and Xeon 6) VM (trust domain) TME-MK AES-XTS with logical integrity TDX module and SGX quoting enclave, Intel Trust Authority TDX Connect (TDISP) SEV-SNP AMD (EPYC Milan onwards) VM AES (SME) and RMP integrity tables; ciphertext hiding (Turin) ASP, VCEK or VLEK through the AMD key distribution service SEV-TIO (TDISP) CCA (Realms) Arm (Armv9-A RME) VM (Realm) Granule protection tables and MEC encryption RSE or HES, CCA platform token RME-DA (device assignment) Secure Execution IBM Z and LinuxONE VM Hardware-encrypted guest memory IBM host-key documents Crypto Express HSM pass-through CSV Hygon (China) VM SEV-derived with SM4 Hygon PSP not stated CoVE and AP-TEE RISC-V (in development) VM Specification-defined TSM attestation CoVE-IO

docs.title: 9.2 Accelerator TEEs and trusted I/O
docs.text: A GPU TEE has to protect three things: the GPU's own memory, the CPU-GPU channel and the GPU-GPU fabric. NVIDIA Hopper solved the CPU-GPU channel with encrypted bounce buffers: the driver inside the confidential VM encrypts transfers with AES-GCM keys negotiated through SPDM, which costs some PCIe throughput. TDISP from PCI-SIG removes this overhead. The device is locked into a trusted state, its configuration is attested, and PCIe IDE encrypts traffic at line rate, so the device's DMA can reach TEE memory directly. Intel TDX Connect, AMD SEV-TIO and Arm RME-DA are the CPU-side halves of that arrangement. Blackwell is NVIDIA's first TEE-I/O-capable GPU, and Vera Rubin NVL72 extends confidential computing across the whole NVLink domain and the CPUs.

docs.title: 9.3 Confidential AI inference end to end
docs.text:
Figure 9.1 follows a confidential inference request. The cloud host OS, hypervisor, BMC and operators are all untrusted. Inside a CPU TEE (a TDX trust domain, SEV-SNP VM or Arm CCA Realm) runs the inference server with a GPU driver in CC mode, an attestation SDK, a vTPM and a guest attestation agent; the decrypted model weights exist only in TEE memory and in the GPU's protected HBM region. The hardware anchors are the CPU's TDX module, ASP or Arm RMM (quotes signed by fused keys), the GPU's on-die RoT with its fused identity and SPDM report, the platform's PRoT, TPM and Caliptra-measured firmware, and the interconnect protections (NVLink encryption, NVSwitch attestation, BlueField-4 ASTRA).

The protocol has six steps. (1) The confidential VM collects the CPU quote and the GPU SPDM report and sends the evidence. (2) A verifier checks vendor certificate chains, measurements, TCB and security version numbers, and debug state. (3) An attestation token (JWT or EAT) is presented to the key broker. (4) The key broker unwraps the model key from the HSM into the TEE only. (5) Encrypted weights are pulled from the store and decrypted inside the VM and GPU. (6) User prompts arrive end-to-end encrypted, and outputs are never visible to the host. The residual risks are physical DRAM interposers (TEE.fail, Battering RAM, WireTap), side channels, attestation-key compromise and a vulnerable guest stack.

Figure 9.1. Confidential AI inference: CPU TEE plus GPU TEE, composite attestation, and attestation-gated release of the model key from an HSM-backed key broker.

docs.text: Category Offerings Hardware-vendor verifiers NVIDIA Remote Attestation Service (NRAS) and the nvTrust local verifier, RIM and OCSP services; Intel Trust Authority; AMD Key Distribution Service (VCEK and VLEK certificates) Cloud attestation and CC services Microsoft Azure Attestation, confidential VMs and confidential GPU VMs; Google Cloud Attestation, Confidential Space, A3 Confidential VMs; AWS Nitro Enclaves attestation with KMS; Oracle and IBM Cloud CC offerings Open source CNCF Confidential Containers (CoCo) and Trustee (key broker and attestation service); Kata Containers; Veraison; Keylime; COCONUT-SVSM; Microsoft OpenHCL paravisor; Enarx Commercial confidential-AI platforms Fortanix, Edgeless Systems (Constellation, Contrast, Privatemode AI), Anjuna Seaglass, Opaque Systems, Decentriq, Tinfoil, Phala Network, Super Protocol, Duality AI-serving integration NVIDIA NIM and Triton in CC mode, vLLM in confidential VMs, Azure AI confidential inferencing, Apple PCC and Meta's private processing as reference designs Industry bodies Confidential Computing Consortium (Linux Foundation), IETF RATS, OCP Security, PCI-SIG, TCG

docs.title: 9.5 Limits of current TEEs
docs.text: Physical memory attacks. Deterministic AES-XTS memory encryption (Intel TDX and SGX scalable mode, AMD SEV-SNP) leaks the equality of ciphertexts. DDR4 and DDR5 interposers (WireTap, Battering RAM, TEE.fail, 2025) extracted secrets and even attestation keys. Mitigations are physical-access controls in AI halls, integrity-protected memory encryption in future CPUs, and short attestation-key lifetimes. Side channels and microarchitecture. Speculative execution, cache, power and frequency side channels (Downfall, CacheWarp, Heckler and others) keep TEE trusted computing bases on a patch-and-re-attest cycle, and verifiers must enforce minimum TCB and security version numbers. Trusted computing base size. The guest OS, drivers, ML frameworks and model-serving code all sit inside the TEE, so a vulnerable inference server leaks weights regardless of hardware. Attestation operations. Reference values (RIMs and CoRIM) and revocation must be fed continuously, and a verifier that accepts anything gives no protection. Accelerator gaps. Many accelerators lack a public TEE, and integrity guarantees may be partial, as in AMD's note on the MI455X against a malicious hypervisor.

docs.title: 9.6 Summary
docs.text:
• Confidential computing keeps weights and prompts encrypted in use, and releases secrets only after remote attestation of a TEE.
  • CPU TEEs (TDX, SEV-SNP, CCA) isolate VMs; GPU TEEs protect GPU memory, the CPU-GPU channel and the GPU-GPU fabric; TDISP with IDE lets devices join the TEE at line rate.
  • In confidential inference the key broker releases the model key from an HSM only against a verified composite attestation of CPU and GPU.
  • Limits remain: physical interposers, side channels, a large TCB, attestation operations and accelerators without a public TEE.

docs.title: 9.7 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why did Hopper need encrypted bounce buffers, and what does TDISP change?

    Answer

    Without a trusted device interface, the CPU-GPU channel had to be protected in software: the driver in the confidential VM encrypts transfers with AES-GCM keys negotiated through SPDM, costing throughput. TDISP locks the device into a trusted state with attested configuration, and IDE encrypts traffic at line rate so DMA can reach TEE memory directly.

  2. In the confidential inference flow, which component decides whether the model key is released, and on what condition?

    Answer

    The key broker with KMS and HSM, which releases the model key only if the policy matches the attested TCB shown in the verifier's attestation token.

  3. Why can an inference-server vulnerability leak weights even on the best hardware?

    Answer

    The guest OS, drivers, ML frameworks and serving code run inside the TEE, so the hardware protects them from outside the TEE but not from bugs in them.

  4. What must a verifier be fed continuously, and why?

    Answer

    Reference values (RIMs and CoRIM) and revocation information. A verifier that accepts anything, or accepts outdated measurements, gives no protection.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Dissecting the Data Centre
docs.text: A data centre is a purpose-built facility that provides conditioned power, cooling, connectivity and physical protection for IT equipment, plus the IT equipment and control software itself. This chapter takes it apart in six zoom levels, from the campus fence to the transistor, and shows that every level has its own controllers, firmware and attack surface. The central idea is that each step inwards trades physical controls for cryptographic ones.

docs.title: 1.1 A stack of nested systems
docs.text:
A data centre is best understood as a stack of nested systems, each with its own controllers, firmware and attack surface. Figure 1.1 zooms from the campus to the silicon. At the outermost level the protections are fences, barriers and guards. At the innermost level they are fuses, keys and sensors on the chip. Between the two, the badges show which classes of security IP are present: a campus has only sensors and anti-tamper measures, a building adds management-plane security, and by the time you reach the server and the chip, roots of trust, key stores, crypto engines, trusted execution and attestation are all present.

Figure 1.1. Dissection of a data centre in six zoom levels, with the classes of security IP present at each level.

The six levels are the campus or site; the building or hall; the row or pod; the rack; the server or tray; and the SoC or chip. The reading of the figure is simple: security that depends on someone standing at a door is replaced, level by level, by security that depends on a key inside a chip.

docs.title: 1.2 Facility subsystems
docs.text:
Facility systems, sometimes called "grey space", are rarely thought of as security IP, yet every one of them is now a networked, firmware-driven device. A compromised UPS, chiller plant or coolant distribution unit can take an AI hall offline faster than any software exploit. The table summarises the main subsystems and what exposes them.

Each of these domains has well-known suppliers (power and cooling from firms such as Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Eaton and Siemens; access control and video from firms such as HID, Genetec and Axis), and the Master Vendor Index at the end of the book lists them with the security function each contributes.

docs.title: 1.3 IT subsystems: the white space
docs.text: The IT equipment lives in the "white space" and has four parts. Compute includes general-purpose servers (x86 from Intel and AMD, and Arm designs such as AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt, NVIDIA Grace and Vera, and Ampere) and accelerated servers (NVIDIA HGX, DGX and NVL72 racks, AMD Instinct, Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Intel Gaudi, Microsoft Maia and Meta MTIA). Storage includes NVMe flash tiers, parallel file systems, object stores and hard-disk archive tiers. Network includes front-end Ethernet, back-end AI fabrics (InfiniBand, Spectrum-X, Ultra Ethernet), scale-up fabrics (NVLink, UALink, AMD Infinity Fabric) and DPUs or SmartNICs. Management includes baseboard management controllers, rack managers, an out-of-band network, jump hosts, privileged-access management, orchestration software (Kubernetes, Slurm, OpenStack), and the identity, key-management and logging services that run the fleet.

docs.title: 1.4 The three control planes
docs.text:
Every data centre runs three logically separate control planes, and attackers look for the seams between them.

Plane What it controls Typical protocols Primary security IP In-band (tenant and data) Workloads, VMs, containers, storage I/O TCP/IP, RDMA, NVMe-oF, TLS CPU and GPU TEEs, link encryption, DPUs Out-of-band (platform) Power on and off, firmware update, console, sensors Redfish, IPMI (legacy), PLDM and MCTP, SPDM, NC-SI BMC secure boot, platform RoT, TPM, DC-SCM Facility OT Power, cooling, fire, physical access BACnet, Modbus, IEC 61850, OPC UA, SNMP Hardened network management cards, OT firewalls, secure elements in cameras and controllers

The out-of-band plane deserves special attention. The BMC that sits on it can switch the machine on and off, reflash its firmware and read its console, so it is the most privileged and most attacked component in the server. Much of the rest of the book is about how to protect it.

docs.title: 1.5 Summary
docs.text:
• A data centre is a stack of nested systems from campus to chip, and each level has its own controllers, firmware and attack surface.
  • Each step inwards trades physical controls for cryptographic ones: fences and guards at the site, keys and fuses in the chip.
  • Facility systems (power, UPS, cooling, building management, physical security, connectivity) are networked, firmware-driven devices and part of the security surface.
  • The white space has compute, storage, network and management parts; the three control planes are in-band, out-of-band and facility OT, and attackers look for the seams between them.

docs.title: 1.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Name the six zoom levels of Figure 1.1 in order, and say which classes of security IP appear at the campus level.

    Answer

    Campus or site; building or hall; row or pod; rack; server or tray; SoC or chip. At the campus level only sensors and anti-tamper measures (badge S) appear.

  2. Why can a compromised cooling distribution unit be as damaging as a software exploit?

    Answer

    CDU and leak-detection controllers are networked devices on protocols such as BACnet, Modbus or Redfish. Tampering with them can cause thermal runaway, taking an AI hall offline faster than a software attack could.

  3. List the three control planes and give one protocol and one security IP block for each.

    Answer

    In-band: for example TLS or RDMA, protected by CPU and GPU TEEs and link encryption. Out-of-band: for example Redfish or SPDM, protected by the BMC secure boot, platform RoT or TPM. Facility OT: for example BACnet or Modbus, protected by hardened network management cards or OT firewalls.

  4. Why is the BMC called the most privileged and most attacked component in the server?

    Answer

    It sits on the out-of-band plane and can power the machine on and off, update firmware and read the console, independent of the host operating system. Compromising it therefore gives control below the level that host security software can see.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Facility, OT and Physical Security
docs.text: Physical security is the outermost layer of defence in depth, and for AI facilities it is a hard dependency of confidential computing: the 2025 interposer attacks show that a technician with brief physical access to a DIMM slot can defeat memory encryption. This chapter describes the concentric protection zones defined by TIA-942 and EN 50600, and the security features to look for in each domain of facility equipment, from access control to operational-technology monitoring.

docs.title: 13.1 Concentric zones
docs.text:
Figure 13.1 shows seven zones from the public approach to the device. Zone 0, public approach: setbacks, landscaping and berms, no signage, drone detection. Zone 1, perimeter: K-rated fence and bollards, crash gates, licence-plate recognition, thermal and PTZ cameras, guard house. Zone 2, building shell: lobby, ID verification, visitor management, blast and ballistic glazing, loading-dock control. Zone 3, secured corridors: badge and PIN, CCTV coverage, anti-passback, NOC and SOC rooms. Zone 4, data hall: biometrics with a mantrap or anti-tailgating portal, escorts, no-media policy. Zone 5, cage or AI pod: customer cages, two-person rule, rack-level electronic locks with audit, CCTV per aisle. Zone 6, device: chassis intrusion detection, tamper-evident seals, self-encrypting drive crypto-erase and RoT anti-tamper sensors. Notice that the last zone is where physical security meets the security IP of the earlier chapters.

Figure 13.1. Concentric physical-security zones from public approach to device, with typical controls.

docs.text:
• Physical security is the outermost layer of defence in depth, and a hard dependency of confidential computing because interposers defeat memory encryption.
  • TIA-942 and EN 50600 define concentric zones from the public approach (zone 0) to the device (zone 6).
  • Each domain of facility equipment has security features to demand: secure credentials, signed firmware, certified network management cards, encrypted OT protocols and passive OT monitoring.

docs.title: 13.4 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why does physical access to a DIMM slot matter for confidential computing?

    Answer

    Interposer attacks in 2025 showed that a technician with brief physical access can defeat memory encryption and even extract attestation keys, so confidential computing is only as strong as the physical security around it.

  2. Which controls of Zone 4 (data hall) address tailgating?

    Answer

    A mantrap or anti-tailgating portal combined with biometrics, plus escorts and a no-media policy.

  3. Why is OSDP Secure Channel preferred to Wiegand for access control?

    Answer

    Wiegand sends credentials in the clear over a simple wire interface; OSDP Secure Channel encrypts and authenticates the reader-to-controller communication.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Interconnect and Network Encryption
docs.text: An AI data centre has at least six distinct encrypted-link technologies, each with its own key management. Data is protected on the wire between the client and the edge, across the fabric, between data centres, between a CPU and its DRAM, between GPUs, and between a device and its host. This chapter maps the technologies onto the data path and lists the standards and the silicon and IP vendors behind each.

docs.title: 10.1 The link-encryption map
docs.text:
Figure 10.1 follows the data path from a client to a remote GPU. From the client to the edge load balancer or API gateway the link uses TLS 1.3 or QUIC with hybrid PQC key exchange. Within the data-centre fabric (leaf and spine) it uses mutual TLS, IPsec or PSP, and MACsec on individual links. Between data centres it uses OTN or 400ZR encryption. Inside the server, a DPU or SuperNIC applies MACsec, IPsec or PSP inline, the CPU encrypts DRAM with AES-XTS (TME-MK, SME or Arm MEC), PCIe IDE with TDISP or bounce buffers protects the CPU-GPU link, NVLink encryption protects GPU-to-GPU traffic, CXL IDE protects CXL memory, and PCIe IDE, NVMe/TCP TLS and self-encrypting drives protect storage. Scale-out RDMA between GPUs uses IPsec or PSP on the SuperNIC, or the Ultra Ethernet transport security sublayer. Each hop has its own key-management plane: TLS PKI, IKE or PSP master keys, MKA (802.1X), IDE_KM over SPDM, and NVLink key exchange under the GPU RoT.

docs.title: 10.3 Summary
docs.text:
• An AI data centre has at least six distinct encrypted-link technologies, each with its own key management.
  • PCIe and CXL IDE (AES-GCM, with TDISP), NVLink and UALinkSec, MACsec, IPsec and PSP, the Ultra Ethernet security sublayer, and layer-1 optical encryption cover the device, fabric and inter-site links.
  • Memory encryption (TME-MK, SME or SEV, MEC) protects DRAM, and self-encrypting drives and OCP L.O.C.K. protect storage at rest.
  • The IDE engines are licensable IP from Synopsys, Rambus, Cadence and others, which is why they appear in so many chips.

docs.title: 10.4 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Name the technology that protects (a) CPU-to-GPU traffic over PCIe, (b) GPU-to-GPU traffic inside a rack, (c) traffic between two data centres.

    Answer

    (a) PCIe IDE with TDISP, or bounce buffers on Hopper. (b) NVLink encryption, or UALinkSec in the open standard. (c) Layer-1 OTN or 400ZR and 800ZR encryption, or MACsec over DWDM.

  2. Why does each hop in the map need its own key-management plane?

    Answer

    The hops use different protocols with different trust endpoints: TLS uses a PKI, IPsec and PSP use IKE or master keys, MACsec uses MKA, IDE keys are programmed with IDE_KM over SPDM, and NVLink exchanges keys under the GPU RoT.

  3. Which cipher family do almost all of the link encryptions in the table use, and which one is the exception for storage and memory?

    Answer

    AES-GCM for the links. Memory and storage use AES-XTS.

  • Chip designers license RoT, crypto, PQC, PUF and IDE IP from a small number of suppliers, led by Synopsys, Rambus, Cadence and open projects.

docs.title: 11.4 Exercises
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a software key manager and an HSM in protecting a model-weight key?

    Answer

    A key manager is a front end that stores and distributes wrapped keys; the HSM is the tamper-responsive, validated vault in which the wrapping keys live and from which they never leave in plaintext.

  2. Why do chip designers license security IP instead of building it?

    Answer

    A correct, side-channel-hardened and validated RoT, crypto engine or IDE module is expensive and specialised. Licensing gives access to tested blocks and, for IDE, to blocks tightly coupled to the vendor's PCIe and CXL controllers.

  3. Which Microsoft component gives every new Azure server a per-server HSM, and what level of validation does it have?

    Answer

    The Azure Integrated HSM, a custom chip with FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation, in every new server from 2025.

docs.title: What this book is
docs.text:
This book is a guided tour of security intellectual property (security IP) in data centres: the silicon blocks, chips, firmware stacks and appliances that provide roots of trust, key storage, cryptography, isolation, attestation and tamper resistance, and the companies and open projects that supply them. It dissects a modern data centre from the campus fence down to the transistor, classifies the main types of data centre, and then concentrates on AI data centres, often called AI factories, where the most valuable asset is no longer customer data alone but the trained model weights.

"Security IP" is used in two senses throughout. The first is licensable semiconductor IP: the RTL blocks, such as a root-of-trust core, an AES engine, a PUF or a PCIe IDE module, that chip designers integrate into a system-on-chip. The second is the wider set of security functions built from that IP and deployed in the facility: TPMs, platform roots of trust, HSMs, trusted execution environments, encrypted links and secure baseboard management controllers.

docs.title: Who it is for and how it fits the library
docs.text: The book is written for students and engineers who already know what a server is and want to understand where the trust comes from. It assumes no cryptography beyond the idea of a key and a signature. It is deliberately distinct from two other guides in the library. The Data Centres guide explains how data centres are powered, cooled, built and run. The Roots of Trust, TPM and PKI guide explains trust anchors, TPMs, secure boot and certificates from first principles. This book sits between them and above them: it maps which security components exist at each level of a data centre, how they fit together in an AI factory, and who builds them. Where a topic is covered at length in those guides, this book gives the short version and points to the idea rather than repeating it.

docs.title: How to read the diagrams
docs.text:
Many figures mark components with lettered badges. They are used in the same way in every chapter.

Badge Meaning R Root of trust (RoT, platform RoT, DICE) K Key storage (TPM, HSM, PUF, OTP) C Crypto engine or link encryption T TEE or confidential computing M Management-plane security (BMC, secure control module) A Attestation (SPDM, DICE certificates) S Sensors and anti-tamper P Post-quantum capable (ML-DSA, ML-KEM, LMS)

docs.title: Scope and currency
docs.text: The material is compiled from public vendor documentation, standards bodies (NIST, TCG, DMTF, OCP, PCI-SIG, the CXL Consortium, CHIPS Alliance) and industry reporting up to October 2026. Roadmap items are marked as such, and some 2026 items are announced rather than generally available. Product names, certification levels and availability change often, so confirm them with the vendor and the primary specification before you rely on them for a design, procurement or compliance decision. Vendor lists are broad but cannot be exhaustive, and inclusion is not an endorsement. Trademarks belong to their respective owners.

docs.title: The seven messages of the book
docs.text:
1. The trust boundary has moved into silicon. In cloud and AI facilities tenants share chips, so security is anchored in hardware roots of trust in every CPU, GPU, NIC, SSD and BMC, and proven remotely through attestation.
  2. A modern server has three tiers of root of trust: a discrete platform RoT, integrated SoC RoTs, and TPMs and HSMs for sealed keys.
  3. Caliptra and OpenTitan are becoming the open default.
  4. AI data centres add GPU-scale confidential computing.
  5. Every link is becoming an encrypted link.
  6. The threat model is now model weights, and physical security still matters.
  7. Post-quantum migration starts in roots of trust, and facility operational technology is part of the attack surface.

Each message has its own chapters, and Chapter 15 pulls them into one reference architecture.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Protecting What Matters: Threats to AI Data Centres
docs.text: Once the facility is understood, the next question is what has to be protected and from whom. For AI data centres the answer has shifted to model weights, and the attackers that matter range from opportunistic criminals to the most capable nation-states. This chapter presents the RAND security levels, the ten classes of threat that converge on the crown jewels with the security IP that mitigates each, and a table of the vulnerabilities from 2021 to 2025 that taught the industry its lessons.

docs.title: 4.1 What must be protected and from whom
docs.text:
The RAND study Securing AI Model Weights (2024) identified 38 attack vectors and defined five security levels, SL1 (amateur attackers) through SL5 (top-priority operations by the most capable nation-states). Frontier AI laboratories now publish security commitments against such levels, with measures such as egress-bandwidth controls and two-party authorisation, and have called for trusted computing on AI accelerators. These map directly onto security IP: confidential computing keeps weights encrypted in use, HSM-wrapped keys with attestation-gated release stop copies of weights from working elsewhere, and roots of trust with attestation keep implanted firmware out of the fleet.

Level Attacker archetype (RAND) Implication for AI data-centre security IP SL1 to SL2 Amateurs, opportunistic criminals Baseline: secure boot, patched BMCs, MFA, encrypted storage SL3 Cybercrime syndicates, insiders Hardware RoT on all platforms, HSM key custody, egress monitoring, two-person rule SL4 Standard nation-state operations Confidential computing for weights, SPDM fleet attestation, supply-chain verification, red teams SL5 Top-priority nation-state operations Isolated, air-gapped-style clusters, TEMPEST and physical hardening, custom verified silicon, no single-person access

docs.text:

docs.title: 4.4 Summary
docs.text:
• The RAND levels SL1 to SL5 grade attackers from amateurs to top-priority nation-states, and each level implies stronger security IP.
  • Ten threat classes converge on the crown jewels; for each there is a primary mitigation (RoT and PFR, platform certificates, confidential computing, DC-SCM, link encryption, signing and SBOM, egress control, OT zoning).
  • Real vulnerabilities teach recurring lessons: firmware implants survive reinstalls, test keys must never ship, multi-tenant GPUs need scrubbing, and cheap physical interposers can defeat memory encryption.

docs.title: 4.5 Exercises
docs.text:
1. At which RAND level does the table first call for confidential computing for weights and SPDM fleet attestation?

    Answer

    SL4, standard nation-state operations.

  2. Why does the BMC vulnerability CVE-2024-54085 reinforce the advice "never expose BMCs"?

    Answer

    It was an authentication bypass in the Redfish interface of a widely used BMC firmware and was added to CISA's known-exploited list. A BMC reachable from a production network can therefore be taken over; the out-of-band network should be isolated.

  3. What do WireTap, Battering RAM and TEE.fail teach about the limits of memory encryption?

    Answer

    Deterministic AES-XTS memory encryption can be defeated by inexpensive DRAM or bus interposers (under USD 1,000), and TEE.fail even extracted attestation keys. Hence physical security of AI halls still matters, alongside integrity-protected memory encryption in future CPUs.

  4. Name three mitigations for the threat class "malicious tenant" and the vulnerabilities that motivate them.

    Answer

    CC modes, MIG isolation, ECC and scrubbing. LeftoverLocals leaked GPU local memory between processes, and GPUHammer used Rowhammer bit-flips to degrade model accuracy.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Reference Architecture and Procurement
docs.text: The earlier chapters described the parts. This last chapter condenses them into an eight-layer defence-in-depth reference architecture for an AI data centre, with minimum and advanced requirements for each layer, a checklist of procurement questions to put to vendors, and a timeline that shows how recently most of this has arrived.

docs.title: 15.1 Eight layers, built from the bottom up
docs.text:
Figure 15.1 stacks eight layers. From the bottom: 1 Silicon (integrated RoT, fuses and PUF, TRNG, crypto and PQC engines, memory encryption, sensors, lifecycle); 2 Device firmware (secure and measured boot, signed and anti-rollback updates, PQC dual signing, OCP recovery); 3 Platform (PRoT with firmware resilience, hardened BMC on DC-SCM, TPM, platform certificates, SPDM fleet attestation); 4 Fabric and interconnect (PCIe and CXL IDE with TDISP, NVLink and UALink encryption, MACsec, IPsec and PSP, isolated out-of-band network); 5 Host and virtualisation (confidential VMs, hardened hypervisor, I/O offload, vTPM); 6 AI workload (encrypted weights and checkpoints, attestation-gated key release, confidential containers, model-registry signing); 7 Security operations (SIEM and XDR, firmware inventory and drift, insider controls, two-person rule, egress limits on weights); 8 Facility and OT (physical zones, IEC 62443 OT segmentation, secure UPS and PDU cards). Across all of them runs governance: NIST 800-193, 800-53 and CSF 2.0, ISO 27001, SOC 2, IEC 62443, FIPS 140-3, CNSA 2.0, the EU CRA and NIS2, and OCP S.A.F.E. The principle is stated at the foot of the figure: trust is built bottom-up, and each layer is only as trustworthy as the measured, attested layer beneath it.

Figure 15.1. Defence-in-depth reference architecture for AI data centres: controls and representative vendors per layer.

docs.title: 15.3 Procurement questions to ask vendors
docs.text:
• Which RoT (vendor, product, version) is in each chip and board, and is its ROM or RTL open or third-party audited (an OCP S.A.F.E. report)?
  • Does every device support SPDM 1.2 or later attestation with a certificate chain to a vendor root, and are reference measurements (RIM and CoRIM) published?
  • What happens on firmware corruption: is there automatic recovery (NIST 800-193 and OCP Recovery) without a technician?
  • Are firmware-signing keys held in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs, and is there a PQC signing roadmap (LMS or ML-DSA) consistent with CNSA 2.0?
  • For GPUs, NICs and SSDs: are CC, TEE-I/O, IDE and TDISP supported in the shipped firmware, and what is the performance cost?
  • Can the owner take ownership of the RoT (owner keys, ownership transfer), and how is the device sanitised at end of life?
  • Which facility controllers (CDU, PDU, UPS, BMS) carry IEC 62443-4-2 or UL 2900 certification, and how are their updates signed?

docs.title: 15.4 A short history
docs.text:
Figure 15.2 is a timeline from 2009 to 2030. It shows how recently the mechanisms of this book arrived: TPM 1.2 and TPM 2.0 (2009 to 2015); Google Titan, Microsoft Cerberus and AWS Nitro (2017); NIST SP 800-193 (2018); OpenTitan and SPDM 1.0 (2019); AMD SEV-SNP, DC-SCM and the TDX specification (2020 to 2021); Caliptra, H100 confidential computing, PCIe 6.0 IDE and TDISP (2022); Intel TDX general availability and OCP S.A.F.E. (2023); the post-quantum FIPS, Blackwell TEE-I/O and Azure Integrated HSM (2024); Caliptra 2.0 and 2.1 with PQC, Lattice MachXO5-NX TDQ, UALink 1.0 and the 2025 interposer attacks (2025); Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale confidential computing, AMD Helios, OpenTitan in production and the Microchip TS1800 (2026); and after that the EU Cyber Resilience Act, fully applicable in December 2027, CNSA 2.0 exclusive post-quantum for firmware signing and networking by 2030, and NIST IR 8547 deprecation of RSA and ECC in 2030 and disallowance in 2035.

Figure 15.2. Timeline of data-centre roots of trust, confidential computing and related standards, 2009 to 2030.

docs.title: 15.5 Summary
docs.text:
• The reference architecture has eight layers: silicon, device firmware, platform, fabric, host, AI workload, security operations and facility, under a governance layer of standards.
  • Trust is built bottom-up: each layer is only as trustworthy as the measured, attested layer beneath it.
  • Minimum requirements (SL2 to SL3) ensure RoTs, signed updates, isolated management and encryption; advanced requirements (SL4 to SL5) add open RoTs, PQC, TDISP and IDE, attested TEEs, HSM-wrapped weight keys, two-person control and continuous attestation.
  • Seven procurement questions turn the architecture into a vendor checklist.

docs.title: 15.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why is "bottom-up" the right way to build the reference architecture?

    Answer

    Each layer relies on measurements and attestation from the layer beneath it. If the silicon and firmware are not trustworthy, nothing above can be, however good the software is.

  2. Name two differences between the minimum and advanced requirements for the platform layer.

    Answer

    Minimum: a NIST 800-193 PRoT or OEM silicon RoT with TPM measured boot, and a BMC never on production networks. Advanced: a DC-SCM whose PRoT aggregates SPDM evidence from every device, and platform certificates verified at receiving.

  3. A vendor says its servers are "secure by design". Write three questions from the checklist to test the claim.

    Answer

    For example: Which RoT is in each chip and is it open or audited (S.A.F.E.)? Does every device support SPDM attestation with published reference measurements? What happens on firmware corruption, and is recovery automatic?

  4. Which regulation becomes fully applicable in December 2027, and what do CNSA 2.0 and NIST IR 8547 require by 2030?

    Answer

    The EU Cyber Resilience Act. CNSA 2.0 requires exclusive post-quantum algorithms for firmware signing and networking equipment by 2030, and NIST IR 8547 (draft) proposes deprecating RSA and ECC by 2030.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Roots of Trust in Practice: Hyperscalers, Open Projects and Products
docs.text: The four largest cloud operators built custom roots of trust between 2017 and 2025, and their designs explain most of today's open standards: Cerberus became the OCP attestation profile, Titan became OpenTitan, and all of them co-founded Caliptra. This chapter surveys those designs, the two open projects Caliptra and OpenTitan in detail, and the commercial products: discrete platform RoTs, integrated RoTs, TPMs and server OEM and ODM implementations.

docs.title: 8.1 Hyperscaler roots of trust
docs.text:
Figure 8.1 compares the architectures of Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS and Apple Private Cloud Compute. Google Cloud puts Titan (2017) on every board as a custom secure MCU that interposes on boot flash, verifies the first instruction and provides fleet identity; Titanium offload silicon with Titan controllers isolates tenant I/O; OpenTitan and Caliptra are the open successors; and Confidential VMs and Confidential Space, Shielded VMs and Cloud HSM provide TEEs, vTPM, measured boot and HSM-backed keys. Microsoft Azure has Project Cerberus (2017), an OCP-contributed NIST 800-193 PRoT on host and BMC flash whose challenge protocol fed into SPDM; the Caliptra 2.0 fleet as an integrated RoT in new silicon, with the Azure Boost offload card and Hydra secure BMC; the Azure Integrated HSM, a per-server FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM chip in every new server (2025 onward); and confidential compute offerings and Managed HSM. AWS has the Nitro cards (all I/O and virtualisation offloaded to Annapurna silicon), the Nitro Security Chip on the mainboard (blocking host writes to non-volatile storage, measuring and updating firmware), the minimal Nitro Hypervisor with NitroTPM and no operator access by design, Nitro Enclaves with signed attestation documents bound to KMS key policy, and always-on DRAM encryption on Graviton. Apple Private Cloud Compute uses Apple-silicon servers with Secure Enclave and signed OS, stateless inference, no privileged runtime access, non-targetability through OHTTP relays and attested-node selection, and verifiable transparency through public logging of every production image.

Figure 8.1. Root-of-trust and isolation architectures of Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS and Apple Private Cloud Compute.

Other operators follow the same pattern. Oracle Cloud pioneered off-box virtualisation and hardware-based firmware re-imaging between bare-metal tenants, so that a RoT wipes and re-verifies firmware before each new customer. Meta runs a private processing service on confidential VMs (AMD SEV-SNP) with confidential GPUs, OHTTP relays and third-party-auditable binaries, an open-industry counterpart to Apple's design. Alibaba Cloud and other Chinese clouds use offload cards, TPM-equivalent TCM and TPCM modules built to GM/T standards with SM2, SM3 and SM4 algorithms, and Hygon CSV, a SEV-derived confidential VM technology.

docs.title: 8.2 Caliptra
docs.text:
Caliptra was announced at the 2022 OCP Global Summit by AMD, Google, Microsoft and NVIDIA and is hosted by the CHIPS Alliance (Linux Foundation). It is an open-source (Apache-2.0) silicon RoT block, delivered as RTL, verification collateral and Rust firmware, that any SoC vendor can integrate so that CPUs, GPUs, NICs, SSD controllers and BMCs all expose the same measurement, identity and attestation behaviour. It is deliberately not a TPM or PRoT replacement: the core is a Root of Trust for Measurement and Identity, and the 2.x subsystem adds the update, recovery and key-management roles.

Figure 8.2 shows the Caliptra 2.x subsystem. The core has a VeeR EL2 RISC-V processor, an immutable boot ROM, SRAM, SHA-2 and SHA-3 engines, HMAC, a KDF and DRBG, ECC P-384, the Adams Bridge PQC accelerator (ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024) with LMS verification, AES-256, a key vault of hardware-only key slots, a PCR vault, a deobfuscation engine for the UDS and field entropy, an entropy source with CSRNG, a mailbox and SoC interface, and a lifecycle-gated JTAG. Around it, a second VeeR core acts as the manufacturer control unit that loads and authorises SoC firmware and runs OCP L.O.C.K. and recovery flows, with an I3C target for OCP streaming boot, a fuse controller for UDS, field entropy, key hashes and security version numbers, and a lifecycle controller (unprovisioned, manufacturing, production, debug-unlocked, RMA). What Caliptra gives the host SoC is a DICE identity chain (IDevID, LDevID, FMC alias and runtime alias), measurement and authorisation of SoC firmware with dual ECC and ML-DSA or LMS signatures, attestation evidence, a hardware key ladder, OCP L.O.C.K. key derivation for SSD controllers, anti-rollback version numbers, debug unlock only with signed tokens, and streaming-boot recovery.

Figure 8.2. Caliptra 2.x subsystem: the core (RISC-V VeeR EL2, crypto, vaults, mailbox) plus MCU, I3C recovery, fuse and lifecycle controllers. Standard in Azure's 2025 fleet 2.1 October 2025 Complete RoT subsystem; Adams Bridge 2.0 adds ML-KEM-1024; ownership transfer of owner-endorsed code; streaming boot for resilient recovery; OCP L.O.C.K. storage key management Adoption 2025 to 2026 Microsoft Azure fleet; AMD products from 2026; ASPEED AST2700 BMC with Caliptra 2.x SiRoT; NVIDIA and Google as founders

docs.title: 8.3 OpenTitan
docs.text:
OpenTitan, launched in 2019 by Google and lowRISC with a coalition of industry and academic partners, is the first open-source silicon RoT built to commercial-grade quality. Earl Grey is the discrete chip (taped out 2023). The first production part, from Nuvoton, shipped in Chromebooks in 2026, with data-centre use as a stated target. Darjeeling is an integratable variant (taped out 2025) that Rivos, now part of Meta, adopted for server SoCs.

Figure 8.3 shows Earl Grey: an Ibex RV32IMCB core in dual-core lockstep, a mask ROM for secure boot, scrambled SRAM and embedded flash, an OTP controller, masked and DPA-hardened AES, HMAC and SHA-2, KMAC and SHA-3, OTBN (a big-number accelerator for RSA, ECC and post-quantum work), an entropy source feeding a CSRNG, a DICE-style key manager, a lifecycle controller, an alert handler with escalation, a sensor controller with voltage, clock, temperature and laser sensors, shadowed registers, SPI host and device for flash pass-through and the usual I/O, with JTAG gated by lifecycle state. Every block is open RTL with design-verification testbenches, formal proofs and a public security model. Earl Grey can act as a platform RoT interposed on SPI flash, as a TPM-like secure element, or as a DICE root for its host.

Figure 8.3. OpenTitan Earl Grey architecture: Ibex core, crypto (AES, HMAC, KMAC, OTBN), key manager, lifecycle, alert handler and sensors.

docs.title: 8.6 TPMs, server OEMs and ODMs, and open firmware
docs.text:
TPM products for data centres come from Infineon (OPTIGA TPM SLB 9672 and 9673, over SPI or I2C, with FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria EAL4+ certification and firmware-upgradable crypto agility), Nuvoton (NPCT75x and NPCT76x), STMicroelectronics (ST33KTPM and ST33TPHF) and Nationz (TCM and TPCM modules, GM/T compliant with SM2, SM3 and SM4, for the Chinese market). Firmware and virtual TPMs (Intel PTT, AMD fTPM, Azure vTPM, Google Shielded VM vTPM, AWS NitroTPM, swtpm) give every VM measured boot and sealed secrets.

OEM or ODM RoT implementation Related features Dell Technologies iDRAC9 and iDRAC10 Silicon Root of Trust (PowerEdge 14G onwards) Secured Component Verification platform certificate, signed firmware, System Lockdown, BIOS live scanning HPE iLO 5, 6 and 7 Silicon Root of Trust; Gen12 iLO 7 secure enclave Gen12 (2025): FIPS 140-3 Level 3 secure enclave, PQC-ready firmware signing, platform certificates, runtime firmware verification Lenovo XClarity Controller 2 and 3 with hardware RoT (NIST SP 800-193 PFR) ThinkShield supply-chain controls, signed firmware, TPM 2.0 Supermicro Hardware RoT (FPGA-based) on X12, H12 and later Secure boot, firmware recovery, TPM, attestation Cisco Trust Anchor module, SUDI (802.1AR) on UCS and Nexus Hardware-anchored secure boot, image signing Oxide Computer NXP LPC55S69 RoT and service processor; no BMC or UEFI Hubris OS, DICE-based attestation, fully open firmware stack ODMs (Quanta, Wiwynn, Foxconn, Inventec, Celestica, Pegatron, GIGABYTE, MiTAC) OCP DC-SCM designs with Lattice, Microchip, ASPEED, Axiado or Caliptra-based RoTs Built to hyperscaler specifications (OCP Attestation, Recovery, S.A.F.E.)

The open-source ecosystem rounds out the picture. Caliptra firmware (in Rust: ROM, FMC and runtime) and OpenTitan ROM and ROM_EXT (C and Rust) are open, with Tock OS as an embedded secure kernel. OpenPRoT is an OCP specification and open-source firmware stack for platform RoTs with a hardware abstraction layer, backed by AMD, Google and other members; AMI's Tektagon OpenEdition PRoT firmware was contributed to OCP in 2022. OpenBMC (Linux Foundation) covers BMCs, with u-bmc and Hubris as alternatives and DMTF libspdm as the reference SPDM stack. For host firmware there are Project Mu, EDK II, coreboot and LinuxBoot, and commercial UEFI from AMI, Insyde and Phoenix.

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Google (Titan), Microsoft (Cerberus), AWS (Nitro) and Apple built custom roots of trust; Cerberus became the OCP attestation profile, Titan became OpenTitan, and all of the big four co-founded Caliptra.
  • Caliptra is an open RoT for measurement and identity with a PQC accelerator in 2.x; OpenTitan is the open discrete (Earl Grey) and integrated (Darjeeling) RoT, first in production silicon from Nuvoton in 2026.
  • Commercial discrete PRoTs come from Lattice, Microchip, ASPEED, Nuvoton and Axiado; integrated RoTs from Intel, AMD, Arm, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers; TPMs from Infineon, Nuvoton and STMicroelectronics.
  • Server OEMs (Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, Cisco) ship silicon RoTs in their BMCs, while ODMs build OCP DC-SCM designs to hyperscaler specifications.

docs.title: 8.8 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Which open projects descend from the proprietary hyperscaler designs, and which standard did Cerberus turn into?

    Answer

    Titan became OpenTitan, and Cerberus became the OCP attestation profile. All of the large clouds also co-founded Caliptra.

  2. Why is Caliptra "deliberately not a TPM or PRoT replacement"?

    Answer

    Its core is a Root of Trust for Measurement and Identity inside a SoC; it measures and identifies the chip. A TPM provides standard storage and reporting, and a PRoT protects platform flash and recovers firmware. The 2.x subsystem adds update, recovery and key management, but the platform still needs a PRoT to aggregate and attest the chips.

  3. What does Caliptra's lifecycle controller enforce, and which states does it have?

    Answer

    It enforces the progress from manufacturing to production to RMA and locks debug ports. The states are unprovisioned, manufacturing, production, debug-unlocked and RMA.

  4. What distinguishes Oxide Computer's design from a conventional server?

    Answer

    It has no BMC and no UEFI: an NXP LPC55S69 acts as RoT and service processor under the Hubris OS, with DICE-based attestation and a fully open firmware stack.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Roots of Trust: Standards and Chains of Trust
docs.text: Part III goes deep on roots of trust. This chapter covers the standards that turn "trust the hardware" into engineering practice, then four mechanisms that every platform root of trust relies on: the boot chain of trust, TCG DICE layering, NIST SP 800-193 platform firmware resilience with an interposing platform RoT, and the SPDM protocol that lets a verifier check any device. It builds on the ideas in the Roots of Trust, TPM and PKI guide, here applied to a server fleet.

docs.title: 7.2 The chain of trust and DICE
docs.text:
Figure 7.1 shows two ideas side by side. In panel A, the platform boot chain, each stage verifies and measures the next. The platform RoT holds the host and BMC in reset, verifies the SPI-flash images against signed manifests and can recover from a golden copy. The BMC boots under secure boot, its images checked by the PRoT before release from reset. The CPU silicon RoT follows (for Intel, microcode and the Boot Guard ACM with an OTP key hash; for AMD, the ASP verifying PSB-signed BIOS; for Arm, the RSE and BL1; for Caliptra, measurement of the SoC firmware). Then come the UEFI firmware (SEC, PEI and DXE, extending PCR0 to 7 in the TPM), UEFI Secure Boot, shim and the bootloader (with db, dbx, KEK and PK signature databases and SBAT revocation), the signed kernel and hypervisor (IMA, EVM, dm-verity), and finally the confidential VM or workload, where remote attestation gates secrets.

Panel B shows TCG DICE layering inside a device. A Unique Device Secret (UDS), fused or derived from a PUF at manufacture, is readable only by the immutable DICE engine and then locked until reset. The engine computes CDI0 from the UDS and a hash of the Layer-0 code and latches UDS access off. Layer 0 derives a DeviceID key pair from CDI0, with a certificate signed by the vendor CA (IDevID) or the owner (LDevID), and computes CDI1 from CDI0 and the hash of Layer 1. Layer 1, the runtime firmware, derives an alias key and an alias certificate that carries the measurements and security version numbers. An attestation responder (SPDM or OCP attestation) then serves the certificate chain and a signed measurement log, and a verifier validates the chain to the vendor root, compares the measurements with reference manifests, applies policy and then releases keys or admits the node to the fleet. The important property is stated in the figure: changing any layer's code changes every CDI and key above it.

Figure 7.1. (A) A server boot chain of trust from PRoT to confidential VM. (B) TCG DICE layering, which gives every chip a measurement-bound identity.

docs.title: 7.3 Platform firmware resilience
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-193 asks a platform to Protect, Detect and Recover. Figure 7.2 shows an active platform RoT doing all three. It sits between the CPU or PCH and the BMC, owns the SPI flash through a mux, filters SPI and eSPI commands to block writes to protected regions, runs crypto (SHA-384, ECDSA-384, AES and, in post-quantum parts, ML-DSA or LMS), controls reset and power sequencing, and filters SMBus or I3C with MCTP and SPDM to attest peripherals. BIOS and BMC flash each hold an active image, a recovery (golden) image and a staging image for updates. Protect means write-protecting the active images and accepting authenticated updates only (signed capsules or PLDM). Detect means verifying every image before releasing the devices from reset, monitoring SPI and SMBus at run time and attesting. Recover means restoring the golden image or streaming new firmware (OCP Recovery), logging the event and re-attesting.

Figure 7.2. Platform Firmware Resiliency: an active PRoT interposes on BIOS and BMC flash, holds devices in reset, and implements Protect, Detect and Recover.

docs.title: 7.4 The DC-SCM
docs.text:
OCP DC-SCM separates the security and management complex from the host processor board. Figure 7.3 shows the split: the host processor module (HPM) carries the CPUs and DIMMs, the PCIe slots, the host SPI flash (or it sits on the SCM), a CPLD or FPGA for power sequencing and the LTPI endpoint, and the voltage regulators, fans and sensors. The secure control module (SCM) carries the BMC SoC, the platform RoT (Caliptra 2.x SiRoT, Lattice, Microchip or OpenTitan), a TPM 2.0 module, the BMC and BIOS flash and eMMC, an LTPI tunnelling CPLD and the management NIC. The two halves meet at the DC-SCI connector.

Figure 7.3. OCP DC-SCM separates the security and management complex (BMC, PRoT, TPM, flash) from the host processor module.

docs.title: 7.5 Device attestation with SPDM
docs.text:
SPDM, the DMTF Security Protocol and Data Model, lets a requester (a PRoT, BMC, host TEE security manager or Caliptra) authenticate and measure a responder (a GPU, NIC, SSD or CXL device) over any bus. Figure 7.4 shows the sequence. The two sides negotiate the version (SPDM 1.2, 1.3 or 1.4) and capabilities (certificates, challenge, measurements, key exchange, mutual authentication) and then the algorithms (ECDSA P-384 with SHA-384, with ML-DSA in 1.4). The requester fetches digests and the certificate chain (the DeviceID and alias chain up to the vendor root CA) and sends a challenge containing a nonce; a signed reply proves possession of the private key. A signed measurements response carries firmware hashes, security version numbers, configuration and debug state. A key exchange (ECDHE) and finish establish a secure session, inside which IDE key programming, TDISP and PLDM firmware update take place. The evidence (certificate chain, measurements and nonce) goes to a verifier, which gives a verdict against reference manifests: admit, quarantine or re-image. SPDM runs over MCTP on SMBus, I2C, I3C, PCIe VDM or USB, over the PCIe or CXL DOE mailbox, or over storage transports such as NVMe-MI.

Figure 7.4. DMTF SPDM device attestation and secure-session establishment, followed by IDE key programming or TDISP.

docs.title: 7.6 Summary
docs.text:
• Standards from NIST, TCG, DMTF, PCI-SIG, the CXL Consortium, OCP, CHIPS Alliance and the IETF turn "trust the hardware" into procurement requirements.
  • In the boot chain each stage verifies and measures the next, from the PRoT through the CPU RoT, UEFI, the OS and finally the confidential workload, where attestation gates secrets.
  • DICE derives a measurement-bound identity: changing any layer's code changes every CDI and key above it.
  • PFR protects, detects and recovers through an interposing PRoT with golden and staging images; SPDM lets a verifier authenticate and measure any device and establish a secure session.

docs.title: 7.7 Exercises
docs.text:
1. In DICE, what happens to the keys above a layer when that layer's code is changed, and why is this useful?

    Answer

    Every CDI and key derived from it changes. A device running modified code therefore cannot produce the identity or alias key it would have with the genuine code, so the change is detected at attestation.

  2. Describe the three parts of NIST SP 800-193 and a mechanism for each in an interposing PRoT.

    Answer

    Protect: write-protect active images and accept only authenticated updates. Detect: verify every image before releasing devices from reset and monitor SPI and SMBus at run time. Recover: restore the golden image or stream new firmware using OCP Recovery, then log and re-attest.

  3. What proves to an SPDM requester that a responder holds the private key of its certificate?

    Answer

    The challenge-response: the requester sends a nonce, and the responder signs it (CHALLENGE and CHALLENGE_AUTH).

  4. A verifier receives signed evidence from a node. What three outcomes can it decide?

    Answer

    Admit the node to the fleet, quarantine it, or re-image it, after comparing the measurements with reference manifests and applying policy.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Supply Chain and Lifecycle Security
docs.text: A root of trust is only as trustworthy as the process that provisioned it. Hyperscalers therefore demand evidence across the full lifecycle: design, wafer fabrication, key injection at the test house, board assembly, shipping, deployment, field updates, RMA and decommissioning. This chapter walks through the stages and the controls, standards and programmes that belong to each.

docs.title: 14.1 Stage by stage
docs.text: Lifecycle stage Controls and standards Vendors and programmes Silicon design and verification Open RTL review (Caliptra, OpenTitan), formal security verification, SCA and fault-injection lab evaluation Cycuity, Caspia, Cadence, Synopsys, Keysight (Riscure), eShard, Brightsight Manufacturing and key injection UDS and IDevID provisioning on HSM-secured test floors; DICE certificate issuance; lifecycle-state locking Rambus CryptoManager, Thales, Entrust, Infineon, Crypto Quantique QuarkLink, Lattice SupplyGuard Firmware review OCP S.A.F.E. (Security Appraisal Framework and Enablement): third-party firmware audits with published short-form reports Review providers such as NCC Group, IOActive and Atredis Partners Board and system assembly TCG platform certificates, 802.1AR IDevID, tamper-evident packaging, component-level SPDM inventory Dell Secured Component Verification, HPE platform certificates, Intel Transparent Supply Chain, Lenovo ThinkShield Software and firmware supply chain SBOM (SPDX, CycloneDX), SLSA, Sigstore, reproducible builds, firmware signing in HSMs Eclypsium, Binarly, Finite State, NetRise; OEM signing services Operation Fleet attestation, firmware drift detection, revocation, runtime monitoring Eclypsium, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (firmware), the hyperscalers' internal fleet systems Decommissioning and RMA Crypto-erase (self-encrypting drives), NIST SP 800-88 sanitisation, RoT ownership transfer and lifecycle RMA state Drive-shredding services, OEM RMA programmes, Caliptra and OpenTitan ownership transfer

docs.title: 14.2 Reading the table
docs.text: Three ideas run through the stages. First, provenance: every device carries an identity (IDevID, DICE certificate, platform certificate) issued under controlled conditions, so a receiving site can check that what arrived is what was built. Second, third-party review: because most firmware is closed, OCP S.A.F.E. gives buyers audit evidence in a standard form, while open RTL (Caliptra, OpenTitan) allows the same scrutiny of silicon. Third, continuity: fleet attestation, drift detection and revocation keep the fleet honest after deployment, and ownership transfer and crypto-erase make sure a device leaves service cleanly. The lifecycle ends where it began, with keys: a decommissioned device that still holds usable keys is a supply-chain risk for whoever receives it next.

docs.title: 14.3 Summary
docs.text:
• A root of trust is only as trustworthy as its provisioning, so evidence is demanded from design to decommissioning.
  • Controls by stage: open RTL review and formal verification; HSM-secured key injection; OCP S.A.F.E. firmware audits; platform certificates at assembly; SBOM and signed builds; fleet attestation in operation; crypto-erase and ownership transfer at the end.

docs.title: 14.4 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Which lifecycle stage does OCP S.A.F.E. address, and what does it give buyers?

    Answer

    Firmware review. It provides third-party firmware audits with published short-form reports.

  2. How does a receiving site check that a server contains the components its manufacturer says it does?

    Answer

    Using platform certificates and 802.1AR identities, with component-level SPDM inventory, for example Dell Secured Component Verification or HPE platform certificates.

  3. What should happen to a device's keys when it is retired?

    Answer

    Crypto-erase (for self-encrypting drives), sanitisation per NIST SP 800-88, and RoT ownership transfer or the RMA lifecycle state, so that no usable keys remain for the next holder.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Post-Quantum Transition
docs.text: A sufficiently large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. For a data centre the immediate worry is not decryption but forgery: an attacker who can forge firmware signatures can load malicious firmware that every root of trust accepts. This chapter explains why roots of trust migrate first, the standards and timelines that drive the migration, the products that already support post-quantum algorithms, and the engineering issues of signing firmware with them.

docs.title: 12.1 Why roots of trust move first
docs.text: Quantum computers capable of breaking RSA and ECC, "cryptographically relevant quantum computers", would let an attacker forge firmware signatures and decrypt recorded traffic. Roots of trust are the first place to migrate because a RoT's verification key is burned into silicon for a decade or more. Equipment bought now stays in service for many years, so every root of trust in it must be able to verify post-quantum signatures, or the fleet carries a weakness that no software update can remove.

docs.title: 12.2 Standards and timelines
docs.text:
NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024, with the stateful hash-based signatures LMS and XMSS in SP 800-208. HQC was selected in 2025 as a backup key-encapsulation mechanism. The NSA's CNSA 2.0 sets the timeline for national-security systems, and NIST IR 8547 (draft) proposes deprecating 112-bit-security RSA and ECC by 2030 and disallowing them by 2035. Software and firmware signing is the first CNSA 2.0 milestone (prefer post-quantum by 2025, exclusively by 2030), and networking equipment follows. Figure 12.1 shows the transition by system category.

Figure 12.1. NSA CNSA 2.0 transition timeline by system category, with NIST IR 8547's proposed RSA and ECC deprecation dates.

docs.title: 12.4 Engineering issues in signing firmware
docs.text:
Moving a firmware chain to post-quantum signatures raises problems that are worth knowing before you read a vendor's claim.

State management. Stateful hash-based signatures such as LMS and XMSS rely on one-time keys. Every server maker, BIOS vendor, BMC vendor and component maker that signs images with them must never reuse a one-time key, which means the signing state has to be tracked and protected, ideally enforced in hardware so that reuse is structurally impossible.

Hybrid operation. Every migration through the mid-2030s will be hybrid, keeping classical algorithms alongside the new ones (dual signatures, hybrid key exchange for TLS and IPsec offload, hybrid secure boot and SPDM attestation), so that a flaw in either family does not break the system.

Algorithm diversity. The standardised schemes are mostly lattice-based. HQC is code-based, so a secret wrapped with both ML-KEM and HQC stays protected even if a weakness is found in lattice cryptography. This matters most for keys that must stay secret for decades, such as archived model weights, backups and long-lived inter-site keys.

Size and speed. Post-quantum signatures are larger than classical ones. Compact schemes would shorten TLS handshakes and SPDM certificate chains over slow management buses, but a safe hardware implementation of the smallest-signature scheme depends on a constant-time sampler, which has delayed its standard.

Side channels. Open roots of trust have shipped lattice engines with limited side-channel protection, and published research in 2025 recovered an ML-DSA key from an open-source root of trust using power analysis. A team integrating a root of trust into a NIC, SSD controller or BMC needs a protected datapath.

Crypto inventory. The first two steps of every migration are to inventory the cryptography in use and to move firmware signing to post-quantum algorithms.

docs.title: 12.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Roots of trust migrate first because their verification keys are fixed in silicon for a decade or more, and forged firmware signatures would defeat every other control.
  • FIPS 203, 204 and 205 (August 2024), SP 800-208 (LMS, XMSS), HQC (2025), CNSA 2.0 and NIST IR 8547 set the algorithms and dates.
  • Caliptra 2.x, Lattice MachXO5-NX TDQ, Microchip TS1800, SEALSQ QS7001 and IP from Rambus, Synopsys, PQShield, CAST and Xiphera already verify post-quantum signatures.
  • Engineering issues: state for hash-based signatures, hybrid operation, algorithm diversity, signature size, side channels and a crypto inventory.

docs.title: 12.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why is a stolen firmware-signing key more worrying than decrypted traffic for a data-centre root of trust?

    Answer

    A forged signature lets an attacker install firmware that every root of trust accepts, giving control below the operating system and surviving reinstalls; decrypting recorded traffic reveals past data but does not give that control.

  2. What must be guaranteed when signing firmware with LMS or XMSS?

    Answer

    Each one-time key must never be reused. The signing state must be tracked and protected, preferably enforced in hardware.

  3. What is the benefit of wrapping a long-lived key with both ML-KEM and HQC?

    Answer

    They rest on different mathematical problems (lattices and codes), so the key stays protected even if a weakness is later found in one family.

  4. According to NIST IR 8547 (draft), when would 112-bit RSA and ECC be deprecated and when disallowed?

    Answer

    Deprecated by 2030 and disallowed by 2035.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Types of Data Centres
docs.text: Data centres are classified by ownership and tenancy, scale, location and workload. These dimensions decide who controls each layer of the stack in Chapter 1, and therefore where the security IP has to sit. This chapter lists the main types, shows how they differ in size and power density, and ends with the practical consequence: the more tenants share the silicon, the more the trust boundary moves from the cage door to the chip.

docs.title: 2.1 Size and density
docs.text:
Figure 2.1 places the major types by facility size (critical IT load, on a log scale from 10 kW to 1 GW) and by rack power density (kW per rack, log scale). A legacy air-cooled rack draws 3 to 8 kW; an NVL72-class AI rack about 120 to 140 kW; and the roadmap for the largest AI systems reaches about 600 kW per rack.

Figure 2.1. Positioning of data-centre types by critical IT load and rack density (indicative ranges, log-log).

The figure carries a summary of what changes for security. Ownership moves from single-tenant (enterprise) to a shared building (colocation) to shared silicon (cloud). The trust boundary moves from the cage door to the chip as multi-tenancy rises. Edge sites have no guards and rely on tamper-evident chassis, TPM or RoT and remote attestation. Hyperscale sites rely on custom roots of trust and supply-chain programmes. AI factories add model-weight protection, GPU TEEs, encrypted scale-up fabrics, liquid-cooling OT and gigawatt-scale power systems.
