docs.title: 2.3 Resilience tiers
docs.text: Availability classification is orthogonal to type. The main schemes are the Uptime Institute Tier I to IV (basic, redundant components, concurrently maintainable, fault tolerant); ANSI/TIA-942 Rated-1 to Rated-4, which also covers physical security and telecom cabling; EN 50600 availability and protection classes in Europe; and the ANSI/BICSI 002 design practices. TIA-942 and EN 50600 both include security zoning requirements, which Chapter 13 describes.

docs.title: 2.4 What the type means for security IP
docs.text: The type determines where the security IP has to be. An enterprise owns its hardware, so it can choose servers with a silicon root of trust (Dell iDRAC, HPE iLO, Lenovo XClarity, Supermicro) and TPM-based measured boot, and it rarely needs confidential computing for internal workloads. In a colocation facility the operator never touches tenant silicon, so security IP sits in the facility (access control, CCTV, OT) and in the tenant's own servers, with shared-responsibility contracts and SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS reports defining the boundary. Hyperscale operators build custom roots of trust (Titan, Cerberus, Nitro, Caliptra), fleet-wide attestation, firmware supply-chain programmes and customer-facing TEEs, and this is where most new security IP originates. The edge assumes physical access by attackers, so it needs anti-tamper sensors, sealed keys and secure zero-touch onboarding (FIDO Device Onboard, IEEE 802.1AR IDevID). AI factories combine hyperscale controls with GPU TEEs, encrypted scale-up fabrics, weight-protection controls (egress limits, two-party access, HSM-wrapped keys) and very high-density power and cooling OT.

docs.title: 2.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Types differ by ownership, tenancy, scale, location and workload, and these decide who controls each layer.
  • The more tenants share silicon, the more the trust boundary moves from the cage door to the chip.
  • Rack density runs from 3 to 8 kW for legacy air-cooled racks to about 120 to 140 kW for NVL72-class racks and about 600 kW on the roadmap.
  • Resilience tiers (Uptime Tier I to IV, TIA-942 Rated-1 to 4, EN 50600) are orthogonal to type; TIA-942 and EN 50600 include security zoning.

docs.title: 2.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Why does a colocation operator have no security IP in the tenant's servers, and where does the operator's security IP sit?

    Answer

    The operator never touches tenant silicon. Its security IP is in the facility: access control, CCTV and OT. The tenant's own servers carry the tenant's security IP, and shared-responsibility contracts and audit reports define the boundary.

  2. A site is an unstaffed edge location in a factory. Which security properties does it need, and why?

    Answer

    It should assume that attackers can reach the hardware: tamper-evident chassis, anti-tamper sensors, TPM or RoT with sealed keys, remote attestation and secure zero-touch onboarding (for example FIDO Device Onboard and IEEE 802.1AR IDevID), because there are no guards to rely on.

  3. Which type of data centre treats model weights and training data as the crown jewels, and what controls does it add to hyperscale controls?

    Answer

    The AI factory (training). It adds GPU TEEs, encrypted scale-up fabrics, weight-protection controls (egress limits, two-party access, HSM-wrapped keys) and high-density power and cooling OT.

  4. Is a Tier IV data centre automatically more secure than a Tier II one? Explain.

    Answer

    No. Availability classification is orthogonal to type and to security. Tier IV means fault tolerance; security requirements such as zoning appear in TIA-942 and EN 50600, not in the Uptime tier itself.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Where the Security IP Sits: The Placement Map
docs.text: Knowing the classes of security IP is not yet knowing where to find them. This chapter places them on an AI server tray, then summarises which classes are standard, optional or absent on each type of data-centre component in products shipping in 2026, and finishes with a component-by-component walkthrough. Read it as a map you can lay over any server you are asked to evaluate.

docs.title: 6.1 Security IP on an AI compute tray
docs.text:
Figure 6.1 places the security functions on a single AI compute tray. The DC-SCM (secure control module) holds the BMC SoC (ASPEED AST2600 or AST2700, Nuvoton NPCM8xx, Axiado TCU) with secure boot, OpenBMC, Redfish and signed updates; the platform RoT (Lattice MachXO3D or MachXO5-NX, Microchip CEC17xx or TS1800, ASPEED AST1060 or AST1080, OpenTitan, Cerberus), which interposes on SPI flash for platform firmware resilience; a TPM 2.0; and optionally a local HSM. The CPUs carry an integrated RoT (Intel CSME and Boot Guard, AMD ASP, Caliptra), a TEE (TDX, SNP or CCA) and AES-XTS memory encryption, and the socket-to-socket link is encrypted in confidential modes. The GPUs carry an on-die RoT and security processor, a fused ECC identity, SPDM, CC mode, an HBM firewall and NVLink or PCIe link encryption. PCIe switches and retimers carry IDE end to end and are attestable, but sit outside the TDISP trusted computing base. DPUs and NICs have their own RoT and IPsec, PSP, MACsec and TLS offload; NVMe SSDs have RoT, self-encrypting AES-XTS, SPDM and OCP L.O.C.K.; CXL memory has CXL IDE and SPDM; and PSUs, fans and CPLDs have signed firmware over PMBus, supervised by the PRoT. Board-level interfaces (SPI and eSPI, I3C and SMBus with MCTP, PCIe DOE, LTPI) and debug ports locked by lifecycle state tie the whole together.

Figure 6.1. Security-IP placement on an AI compute tray: DC-SCM (BMC, PRoT, TPM), CPUs, GPUs, PCIe fabric, DPU, SSDs, CXL memory and power.

docs.title: 6.2 The heat map
docs.text:
Figure 6.2 is a heat map of which classes of security IP are standard, optional or rare on each type of data-centre component in current shipping products. The rows are the components (server CPU, GPU or AI accelerator, DPU or SmartNIC, scale-out NIC, switch ASIC, scale-up switch, NVMe SSD, HDD, CXL memory expander, PCIe switch or retimer, BMC SoC, PSU, FPGA or CPLD, rack manager or CDU controller, UPS or PDU network card, access control and CCTV) and the columns are the classes (integrated RoT, discrete PRoT, TPM, HSM, fuses and PUF, secure and measured boot, SPDM attestation, memory and at-rest encryption, link encryption, TEE, PQC support, tamper sensors).

Figure 6.2. Heat map of security IP by data-centre component (state of shipping products, 2026).

docs.title: 6.3 Component by component
docs.text:
Server CPUs. Every current server CPU contains an integrated security processor: the AMD Secure Processor (Arm-based, running SEV firmware and Platform Secure Boot); Intel CSME and Server Platform Services plus microcode-enforced Boot Guard and the TDX module; Arm Neoverse designs with TrustZone, the Runtime Security Engine and the Realm Management Extension of CCA; and hyperscaler Arm CPUs (Graviton, Axion, Cobalt) anchored by Nitro, Titan and Cerberus or Caliptra respectively. Memory encryption is built in, and AMD and others are adding Caliptra as the standard measurement RoT from 2026.

GPUs and AI accelerators. NVIDIA GPUs since Hopper contain a hardware RoT, a RISC-V-based GPU system processor and security microcontrollers, fused device-identity keys with an NVIDIA-rooted certificate chain, SPDM responders and the CC-mode firewall that walls off a protected HBM region. Blackwell adds TEE-I/O and NVLink protection, and Rubin extends this to rack scale. AMD Instinct uses the AMD Secure Processor lineage and DICE identities. Custom accelerators (TPU, Trainium, Maia, MTIA) rely on platform RoTs and hyperscaler offload cards.

DPUs, SmartNICs and SuperNICs. DPUs are full computers with their own RoT and secure boot: NVIDIA BlueField-3 and BlueField-4 (hardware RoT, IPsec, TLS and MACsec offload, ASTRA on BlueField-4), AMD Pensando, Intel IPU, Marvell OCTEON 10, Broadcom Stingray and Thor, and hyperscaler cards (AWS Nitro, Azure Boost, Google Titanium). They terminate tenant encryption and enforce isolation off the host, which makes them among the most security-critical chips in an AI data centre.

Network switch ASICs. Switch silicon generally provides secure boot of the switch CPU and operating system, often with a TPM and a CPLD or FPGA RoT on the board, and MACsec on many ports or PHYs. Network operating systems (Arista EOS, Cisco NX-OS, Junos, SONiC) add signed images and IEEE 802.1AR device identities.

NVMe SSDs and HDDs. Enterprise SSD controllers integrate a RoT, AES-256-XTS self-encryption (TCG Opal 2 or Ruby), crypto-erase and SPDM attestation, as required by the OCP Datacenter NVMe SSD specification. OCP L.O.C.K., built on Caliptra, moves media-encryption-key handling into an open, auditable RoT so that keys never exist outside it in plaintext.

CXL memory and the PCIe fabric. CXL Type-3 memory expanders implement CXL IDE and SPDM where supported. PCIe switches and retimers carry their own secure boot and attestation and pass IDE-encrypted traffic end to end.

BMC and DC-SCM. The BMC is the most privileged and most attacked component in the server. Current SoCs have secure boot, crypto engines and OTP keys; the ASPEED AST2700 adopts a Caliptra 2.x silicon RoT with streaming boot over LTPI. OCP DC-SCM moves the BMC, PRoT and TPM onto a replaceable module, described in Chapter 7.

PSUs, fans, CPLDs and FRUs. Power-supply microcontrollers increasingly support signed firmware and SPDM. Secure authenticators (for example Analog Devices DeepCover, Microchip ATECC608, Infineon OPTIGA Trust, NXP EdgeLock) verify field-replaceable units and cables. CPLDs and FPGAs handle power sequencing and often host the PRoT logic (Intel PFR).

Rack and facility controllers. Rack managers, CDUs, PDUs and UPS network cards are embedded Linux or RTOS devices. Look for secure boot, signed firmware, IEC 62443-4-2 or UL 2900 certification, and Redfish with TLS and per-device certificates. Cameras and access controllers increasingly embed secure elements.

docs.title: 6.4 Summary
docs.text:
• The placement map shows every chip on an AI tray with its own security function: the DC-SCM holds the BMC, PRoT and TPM; CPUs, GPUs, DPUs, SSDs and CXL memory each carry an RoT or identity; PSUs and CPLDs have signed firmware.
  • Every current server CPU has an integrated security processor; every NVIDIA GPU since Hopper has an on-die RoT and CC mode; DPUs are among the most security-critical chips.
  • The BMC is the most privileged and most attacked component, which is why it is moved onto a replaceable DC-SCM with its own RoT.
  • Facility controllers need secure boot, signed firmware, IEC 62443-4-2 or UL 2900 certification and Redfish with TLS.

docs.title: 6.5 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Which components sit on a DC-SCM, and why is putting them on a replaceable module attractive?

    Answer

    The BMC, the platform RoT and the TPM (with flash). The module separates the security and management complex from the host processor board, so it can be standardised, replaced or upgraded independently.

  2. Why are DPUs described as among the most security-critical chips in an AI data centre?

    Answer

    They are full computers with their own RoT and secure boot that terminate tenant encryption and enforce isolation off the host, so a compromise would undermine both.

  3. What does OCP L.O.C.K. change about how an SSD handles media-encryption keys?

    Answer

    It moves key handling into an open, auditable RoT built on Caliptra, so that the keys never exist outside it in plaintext.

  4. PCIe switches carry IDE-encrypted traffic end to end. Are they inside the trusted computing base of TDISP?

    Answer

    No. They can be attested, but sit outside the TDISP trusted computing base.
